newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac flies home to French shambles.
newsitem.headline: Chirac flies home to French shambles.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac flew home on Friday from a state visit to Japan to a France in political turmoil, hit by a new bout of monetary jitters and with angry truck drivers blockading many of the highways.

During his six-day jaunt as a travelling salesman for French exports to Asia's biggest economy, his domestic situation has worsened to a point where radio commentator Catherine Nay compared it jokingly to a coup bid in the absence of an African dictator.

In a conflict reminiscent of last year's 24-day rail strike, striking lorry drivers have paralysed many provincial towns by using their trucks to blockade motorways, key bridges and fuel depots to demand pay rises, shorter hours and early retirement.
The five-day-old action has started to hit the economy, with petrol stations running dry in some cities.

Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing's call on Wednesday for an effective devaluation of the franc has hit the French currency and reignited open warfare in Chirac's centre-right coalition over the future single European currency.
Jubilant Eurosceptics, led by Gaullist heavyweights Philippe Seguin and Charles Pasqua, rushed to hail the co-founder of the European Monetary System in 1978 as a convert to their cause.

"Mr Giscard d'Estaing's analysis meets mine and above all that of the French people, who are questioning in increasing numbers a policy devoted solely to the creation of the euro in unfavourable conditions for the economy, investment and jobs," said Pasqua.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had to issue a joint statement reaffirming their commitment to launching the single currency on time in 1999 and saying the current franc-mark exchange rate reflected economic reality.

Coming from a senior advocate of the Maastricht treaty, Giscard d'Estaing's bombshell broke a taboo, allowing supporters of monetary union to question the long-untouchable "franc fort" (strong franc) policy.
The government, floundering against record 12.6 percent unemployment, is in a weak position to resist such a challenge.

Juppe's approval rating slumped to the lowest in the history of the Fifth Republic on Tuesday, prompting speculation about an imminent cabinet reshuffle, perhaps as early as next week. A poll found only 22 percent of voters approve of his performance.

That fuelled talk in parliament of cabinet changes, possibly as early as next week, which Chirac's statement in Tokyo that he would stay the course of deficit-cutting and accept the unpopularity did little to damp down.
Aides of Chirac and Juppe sought to dismiss the speculation, saying a reshuffle would probably only happen at the turn of the year or in early 1997.

The aim would be to unite the coalition by bringing in key supporters of former prime minister Edouard Balladur, Chirac's unsuccessful fellow-Gaullist rival in last year's presidential election, in the run-up to a general election due in March 1998.

But the monetary row has complicated that effort, with Chirac now facing conflicting pressures from centrists who want him to appoint a more enthusiastically pro-European team and sack supporters of Seguin and Giscard d'Estaing, and from Eurosceptics who want him to dump Juppe.
